title: Chapter 48 — The First Lowering
paragraphs: The phantoms, for so they then seemed, were flitting on the other side of the deck, and, with a noiseless celerity, were casting loose the tackles and bands of the boat which swung there. This boat had always been deemed one of the spare boats, though technically called the captain's, on account of its hanging from the starboard quarter. The figure that now stood by its bows was tall and swart, with one white tooth evilly protruding from its steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton funereally invested him, with wide black trousers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning this ebonness was a glistening white plaited turban, the living hair braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less swart in aspect, the companions of this figure were of that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manillas — a race notorious for a certain diabolism of subtlety, and by some honest white mariners supposed to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents on the water of the devil, their lord, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.
While the wondering ship's company were still staring at these strangers, Ahab cried out to the white-turbaned old man at their head, "All ready there, Fedallah?"
"Ready," was the half-hissed reply.
"Lower away then, do you hear?" shouting across the deck. "Lower away there, I say."

Such was the thunder of his voice that, despite their amazement, the men sprang over the rail. The pulleys whirled round in the blocks. With a lurch, the three boats dropped into the sea. And with a daring agility unknown in any other profession, the sailors leaped like goats down the rolling ship's side into the tossing boats below.

They had hardly pulled out from under the ship's shelter when a fourth boat, coming from the windward side, pulled around under the stern and revealed the five strangers rowing Ahab, who stood erect in the stern and loudly ordered Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask to spread themselves widely so as to cover a large stretch of water. But with all their eyes riveted upon the dark Fedallah and his crew, the men in the other boats did not obey the command.
"Captain Ahab? —" said Starbuck.
"Spread yourselves," cried Ahab. "Give way, all four boats. You, Flask, pull out more to leeward!"

"Aye, aye, sir," cheerily cried little King-Post, sweeping his great steering oar around. "Lay back!" he called to his crew. "There! — there! — there again! There she blows right ahead, boys! — lay back!"
"Never mind those yellow fellows, Archy."
"Oh, I don't mind them, sir," said Archy. "I knew it all before. Didn't I hear them in the hold? And didn't I tell Cabaco here about it? What do you say, Cabaco? They are stowaways, Mr. Flask."

"Pull, pull, my fine hearts-alive; pull, my children; pull, my little ones," drawlingly and soothingly sighed Stubb to his crew, some of whom still showed signs of uneasiness. "Why don't you break your backbones, my boys? What is it you stare at? Those chaps in yonder boat? Tut! They are only five more hands come to help us — never mind from where — the more the merrier. Pull, then, do pull; never mind the brimstone — devils are good fellows enough. So, so; there you are now; that's the stroke for a thousand pounds; that's the stroke to sweep the stakes! Hurrah for the gold cup of sperm oil, my heroes! Three cheers, men — all hearts alive! Easy, easy; don't be in a hurry — don't be in a hurry. Why don't you snap your oars, you rascals? Bite something, you dogs! So, so, so, then — softly, softly! That's it — that's it! long and strong. Give way there, give way! The devil fetch ye, ye ragamuffin rapscallions; ye are all asleep. Stop snoring, ye sleepers, and pull. Pull, will ye? pull, can't ye? pull, won't ye? Why in the name of gudgeons and ginger-cakes don't ye pull? — pull and break something! pull, and start your eyes out! Here!" — whipping out the sharp knife from his girdle — "every mother's son of ye draw his knife, and pull with the blade between his teeth. That's it — that's it. Now ye do something; that looks like it, my steel-bits. Start her — start her, my silver-spoons! Start her, marling-spikes!"

Stubb's exordium to his crew is given here at large because he had rather a peculiar way of talking to them in general, and especially in inculcating the religion of rowing. But you must not suppose from this specimen of his sermonizings that he ever flew into downright passions with his congregation. Not at all; and therein consisted his chief peculiarity. He would say the most terrific things to his crew in a tone so strangely compounded of fun and fury, and the fury seemed so calculated merely as a spice to the fun, that no oarsman could hear such queer invocations without pulling for dear life, and yet pulling for the mere joke of the thing. Besides he all the time looked so easy and indolent himself, so loungingly managed his steering-oar, and so broadly gaped — open-mouthed at times — that the mere sight of such a yawning commander, by sheer force of contrast, acted like a charm upon the crew. Then again, Stubb was one of those odd sort of humorists, whose jollity is sometimes so curiously ambiguous, as to put all inferiors on their guard in the matter of obeying them.
In obedience to a signal from Ahab, Starbuck was now pulling diagonally across Stubb's bow. When for a minute or so the two boats were fairly near each other, Stubb hailed the mate.
"Mr. Starbuck! Portside boat there, ahoy! A word with you, sir, if you please!"
"Hello!" returned Starbuck, turning not a single inch as he spoke, still earnestly but in whispers urging his crew, his face set like flint away from Stubb's.
"What do you think of those yellow fellows, sir?"

"Smuggled on board, somehow, before the ship sailed. (Strong, strong, boys!)" in a whisper to his crew, then speaking out loud again: "A sad business, Mr. Stubb! (Drive her, drive her, my lads!) But never mind, Mr. Stubb, all for the best. Let all your crew pull strong, come what may. (Spring, my men, spring!) There's barrels of sperm ahead, Mr. Stubb, and that's what we came for. (Pull, boys!) Sperm, sperm's the game! This at least is duty — duty and profit hand in hand."

"Aye, aye, I thought as much," Stubb said to himself when the boats diverged. "As soon as I clapped eyes on them, I thought so. Aye, and that's what he went into the after-hold for so often, as Dough-Boy long suspected. They were hidden down there. The White Whale's at the bottom of it. Well, well, so be it! Can't be helped! All right! Give way, men! It isn't the White Whale today! Give way!"

Now, the advent of these outlandish strangers at such a critical instant as the lowering of the boats from the deck had not unreasonably awakened a sort of superstitious amazement in some of the ship's company; but Archy's fancied discovery having some time previous got abroad among them, though indeed not credited then, this had in some small measure prepared them for the event. It took off the extreme edge of their wonder; and so what with all this and Stubb's confident way of accounting for their appearance, they were for the time freed from superstitious surmisings; though the affair still left abundant room for all manner of wild conjectures as to dark Ahab's precise agency in the matter from the beginning. For me, I silently recalled the mysterious shadows I had seen creeping on board the Pequod during the dim Nantucket dawn, as well as the enigmatical hintings of the unaccountable Elijah.

Meantime, Ahab, out of hearing of his officers, having sided the furthest to windward, was still ranging ahead of the other boats — a circumstance bespeaking how potent a crew was pulling him. Those tiger yellow creatures of his seemed all steel and whalebone; like five trip-hammers they rose and fell with regular strokes of strength, which periodically started the boat along the water like a horizontal burst boiler out of a Mississippi steamer. As for Fedallah, who was seen pulling the harpooneer oar, he had thrown aside his black jacket, and displayed his naked chest with the whole part of his body above the gunwale, clearly cut against the alternating depressions of the watery horizon; while at the other end of the boat Ahab, with one arm, like a fencer's, thrown half backward into the air, as if to counterbalance any tendency to trip, Ahab was seen steadily managing his steering oar as in a thousand boat lowerings ere the White Whale had torn him. All at once the outstretched arm gave a peculiar motion and then remained fixed, while the boat's five oars were seen simultaneously peaked. Boat and crew sat motionless on the sea. Instantly the three spread boats in the rear paused on their way. The whales had irregularly settled bodily down into the blue, thus giving no distantly discernible token of the movement, though from his closer vicinity Ahab had observed it.
"Every man look out along his oars!" cried Starbuck. "You, Queequeg, stand up!"

Nimbly springing up on the triangular raised platform in the bow, the harpooner stood erect there, and with intensely eager eyes gazed off toward the spot where the chase had last been seen. Likewise upon the extreme stern of the boat, where it was also triangularly raised level with the gunwale, Starbuck himself was seen coolly and skillfully balancing himself against the jerking tosses of his chip of a craft, silently scanning the vast blue eye of the sea.

Not very far off, Flask's boat was also lying breathlessly still. Its commander was recklessly standing upon the top of the loggerhead, a stout post rooted in the keel and rising some two feet above the level of the stern platform. It is used for catching turns with the whale line. Its top is no bigger than the palm of a man's hand, and standing on such a base, Flask seemed perched at the masthead of some ship that had sunk to all but her topmost spars. But little King-Post was a resourceful fellow. Not a man to be long kept down by anything. And though the huge Daggoo loomed behind him like a dark mountain, Flask would still be the first to see a whale.
"I can't see three waves off. Tip us up an oar there and let me climb on that."
Upon this, Daggoo, with either hand on the gunwale to steady himself, swiftly slid to the stern, and then straightening up, volunteered his lofty shoulders as a pedestal.
"Good a masthead as any, sir. Will you mount?"
"That I will, and thank you very much, my fine fellow. Only I wish you were fifty feet taller."

Whereupon, planting his feet firmly against two opposite planks of the boat, the gigantic harpooner stooped a little, presented his flat palm to Flask's foot, and then, putting Flask's hand on his plumed head and telling him to spring as he himself should toss, with one skillful fling landed the little man high and dry on his shoulders. And there was Flask now standing, with Daggoo's one lifted arm providing him with a chest-strap to lean against and steady himself.

At any time it is a strange sight for the newcomer to see with what marvelous habitual skill the whaleman will keep an upright posture in his boat, even when pitched about by the most violently contrary seas. Stranger still to see him perched giddily on the loggerhead itself under such conditions. But the sight of little Flask mounted on gigantic Daggoo was even more remarkable. For supporting himself with a cool, indifferent, effortless, almost savage majesty, the noble black — to all appearances — bore little Flask on his shoulders with as much easy pride as though the little man were simply a badge or ornament he wore. So that they seemed like the black figure on the front of some enormous hearse, bearing a white coffin.

Meanwhile Stubb, the third mate, betrayed no such far-gazing anxieties. The whales might have made one of their regular deep dives, not a temporary plunge from mere fright. And if so, Stubb, as was his habit in such cases, was resolved to comfort the waiting interval with his pipe. He pulled it from his hatband, where he always wore it at an angle like a feather. He loaded it and tamped down the tobacco with his thumb. But he had barely lit his match on the rough sandpaper of his hand when Tashtego, his harpooner, whose eyes had been set on a level with the water like two floated pistols, gave a sharp shout and declared that the whale was just below. Instantly, Stubb's pipe went out of his mouth.

To a landsman, no whale, nor any sign of a herring, would have been visible at that moment — nothing but a troubled patch of greenish-white water and thin scattered puffs of vapor hovering over it, blowing off to leeward like confused spray from white-capped waves. The air around suddenly vibrated and tingled, as it does above intensely heated iron plates. Beneath this atmospheric wavering and curling, and partially beneath a thin layer of water too, the whales were swimming. Seen through the warped air and water, their vast dim shapes looked strangely magnified, like the full-length reflections in a thin mirror. No wonder there had been some among the hunters who, transported and bewildered by such an enchanted sight, had fatally mistaken the size of the whale and struck too close. And so been dragged down into the deep, crushed by the weight of the rising monster.

All four boats were now in keen pursuit of that one spot of troubled water and air. But it seemed ready to outrun them. It flew on and on, like a mass of merging bubbles swept down a swift stream from the hills.

"Pull, pull, my good boys," said Starbuck, in the lowest possible but most intensely concentrated whisper to his men. The sharp fixed glance from his eyes, aimed straight ahead of the bow, seemed almost like two visible needles in two unerring compasses. He did not say much to his crew, nor did they say anything to him. Only the silence of the boat was at intervals piercingly broken by one of his peculiar whispers — now harsh with command, now soft with pleading.

How different the loud little King-Post. "Sing out and say something, my hearties! Roar and pull, my thunderbolts! Beach me, beach me on their black backs, boys! Only do that for me, and I'll sign over my Martha's Vineyard plantation to you, boys — including wife and children! Lay me on — lay me on! Oh Lord, Lord! I'll go stark, staring mad! See! See that white water!" And shouting, he pulled his hat from his head and stomped up and down on it. Then he picked it up and flung it far off upon the sea. And still he shrieked: "Lay me on — lay me on! Lay me on, sir!" he cried to Daggoo. "Break something! Break your back! Burst yourself! Only get me there!"

"Look at that fellow now," Stubb drawled philosophically, following along at a short distance with his unlit pipe still mechanically clamped between his teeth. "He's got fits, that Flask has. Fits? Yes, give him fits — that's the very word — pitch fits into them. Merrily, merrily, hearts alive! Pudding for supper, you know — merry's the word. Pull, babes — pull, sucklings — pull, all. But what the devil are you hurrying about? Softly, softly, and steadily, my men. Only pull, and keep pulling. Nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two — that's all. Take it easy — why don't you take it easy, I say, and burst all your livers and lungs!"

But what it was that inscrutable Ahab said to that tiger-yellow crew of his — those are words best left unspoken here, for you live under the blessed light of the Christian land. Only the godless sharks in the lawless seas may hear such words, when, with a tornado brow and eyes of red murder and foam-glued lips, Ahab leaped after his prey.

Meanwhile, all the boats tore on. The repeated specific references Flask made to "that whale" — as he called the imaginary monster he declared was constantly teasing his boat's bow with its tail — these references were at times so vivid and lifelike that they would cause one or two of his men to steal a fearful look over their shoulders. But this was against all rules. The oarsmen must row blindly, their eyes shut and a skewer through their necks — custom dictating that they must have no sight of the terror facing them. Well enough for them. But what about us in the bow? We could see the whole thing.

It was a sight full of sudden wonder and awe! The vast swells of the all-powerful sea, the surging hollow roar they made as they rolled along the eight gunwales like gigantic bowls in a boundless bowling green, the brief suspended agony of the boat as it tipped for an instant on the knife-like edge of the sharper waves that almost seemed about to cut it in two, the sudden profound plunge into the watery valleys, the keen goading surges to gain the top of the opposite hill — all this was thrilling. Not a man breathed. A thin mist of sweat covered every face. The chests heaved as if laboring at the forge. Not one word was spoken.

Not the raw recruit, marching from the arms of his wife into the fever heat of his first battle — not the dead man's ghost encountering the first unknown phantom in the other world — neither of these can feel stranger and stronger emotions than the man who for the first time finds himself pulling into the charmed, churning circle of the hunted sperm whale.

The dancing white water made by the chase was now becoming more and more visible, owing to the deepening darkness of the cloud-shadows on the sea. The jets of spray no longer blended, but tilted everywhere to right and left. The whales seemed to be separating their paths. The boats were pulled farther apart. Starbuck gave chase to three whales running dead to leeward. Our sail was now set, and with the still-rising wind we rushed along — the boat going with such fury through the water that the lee oars could barely be dipped in time to escape being torn from the row-locks.
Soon we were running through a wide, drifting veil of mist. Neither ship nor boat to be seen.
"Give way, men," whispered Starbuck, drawing the sheet of his sail still further aft. "There is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There's white water again! — close by! Spring!"

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us told us the other boats had struck fast. But they were hardly heard when, with a lightning-fast hissing whisper, Starbuck said: "Stand up!" and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was facing the life-and-death danger so close ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense face of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew the critical instant had come. They heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound, as of fifty elephants stirring in their bedding. Meanwhile the boat was still racing through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the raised crests of enraged serpents.
"That's his hump. There, there, give it to him!" whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat — it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from behind, while forward the boat seemed to strike a ledge. The sail collapsed and exploded. A gush of scalding steam shot up nearby. Something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew was half-suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together. And the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

Though completely swamped, the boat was nearly unharmed. Swimming around it, we picked up the floating oars, and lashing them across the gunwale, tumbled back to our places. There we sat up to our knees in the sea, the water covering every rib and plank, so that to our downward-gazing eyes the suspended craft seemed a coral boat grown up to us from the ocean floor.

The wind increased to a howl. The waves dashed their shields together. The whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire upon the prairie, in which, unconsumed, we were burning — immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats. You might as well roar down the chimney of a blazing furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving spray, scud, and mist grew darker with the shadows of night. No sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea made an eerie sound against the half-submerged gunwale. At times we had to bail the boat with our hats. The oars were useless as propellers. We were forced to use them as paddles, guiding the boat through the breakers. Each man sat with his back to the sea, his face turned upon the others, and each flashing cheek was his companion's lightning-rod.

Wet, drenched through, and shivering cold, despairing of ship or boat, we lifted our eyes as dawn came. The mist still spread over the sea. The empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg started to his feet, cupping his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, as of ropes and masts hidden by the storm. The sound came nearer and nearer. The thick mists were dimly parted by a huge, vague form. Terrified, we all sprang into the sea as the ship, which at last had been searching for us after the other boats returned, bore directly down upon us within a distance of not much more than its own length.

Floating on the waves we watched the abandoned boat as it tossed and gaped beneath the ship's bow like a wood chip at the base of a waterfall. Then the vast hull rolled over it, and it was seen no more until it came up wallowing astern. Again we swam for it, were dashed against it by the seas, and were at last pulled up and safely landed on board. Before the squall hit, the other boats had cut loose from their fish and returned to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up, but was still cruising back and forth in case any sign of us should appear. It was only the morning after that we were recovered.
